title: The king and the Goddess
hookLine: the wind can't move a blade of grass; the stranger vanishes before Indra, and the Goddess Uma appears to teach him
carry: the divine mother reveals what the gods couldn't

lines: THE NEXT ONE WILL CRACK IT.
cards: Fire came back empty-handed, and the gods are sure the next one will crack it. He's stronger. He has more reach.
And when he fails too, they send their king. What happens to the king is the strangest turn in the whole story, because he doesn't fail the way the others did.

teach.b: The gods turn to Vayu, the wind. Vayu, find out what this wondrous being is. He runs up.
Who are you? I am Vayu, the one who moves through the sky. What power is in you?
I could carry off everything there is, whatever is on this earth. The same blade of grass is set down. Carry this off.
Vayu rushes at it with all his speed, and can't move it.

teach.h: THE KING COMES, AND IT VANISHES.
teach.b: He comes back: I couldn't find out. Then the gods turn to Indra, their king. Maghavan, find out what this being is.
Indra runs toward it, and the being vanishes. No test. Just gone.
Why? The text doesn't say. One common reading: Indra was the proudest, the king, so he's made to wait and learn humility.
Either way, the king is left standing in empty space.
And there, in that same space, he meets a woman, very radiant, and the text names her: Uma, daughter of Himavat, the Himalaya.
It's among the earliest times Uma appears by name, and many Hindus hear in her the goddess Parvati, the divine mother.

teach.h: THE GODDESS KNOWS WHAT THE GODS DON'T.
teach.b: Indra asks her what none of the gods could answer: what was that being? Notice who knows. Not fire, not wind, not the king.

Many Hindus, especially those who worship the Goddess as Shakti, read it this way: the highest truth is shown through the Mother. It's one reason so many Hindus, when their own strength runs out, simply call: Ma.

how: Many Hindus, especially in Shaiva and Shakta traditions, honor Uma Haimavati in the Kena as an early appearance of the goddess, the divine mother who teaches the gods.

o: Uma, the radiant daughter of the Himalaya
the queen of the gods, Indra's wife
a mountain spirit who guards the snows

games.q: who did what in the story — tap the pairs.
p: the wind; couldn't move the grass
king of the gods; the being vanished

s: the being tested Indra with the blade of grass too
for Indra it simply vanished; no question, no test.
Uma in the Kena is often identified with Parvati
many Hindus hear in Uma Haimavati the goddess, Shiva's consort.
the Kena explains why the being vanished
it doesn't say; one common reading is that the proud king had to learn humility.

games.q: fire and wind have failed, and the king came up empty. in the Kena, who finally knows what the being was?
o: Uma, the radiant Goddess, daughter of the Himalaya.
games.why: Uma knows what fire, wind and the king couldn't. many Hindus read it as the highest truth shown through the divine mother.

practice: Think of a time your own strength ran out: an answer you couldn't find, a plan that slipped away. Stay with that empty space without rushing to fill it. In the story, that's exactly where the teacher appears.
If you pray, call on the Mother, as many Hindus do, simply Ma, and wait. If you don't, think of someone who taught you what you couldn't get alone, and thank them silently.

wordCard.voice: Uma Haimavati, Uma, daughter of Himavat. The wind cannot move the grass; the king comes near and the being vanishes; and there, Indra meets Uma, radiant, daughter of the Himalaya.

orig.note: Sanskrit: Uma Haimavati, Uma, daughter of Himavat, the Himalaya.

carryVoice: Your line: the divine mother reveals what the gods couldn't. Her answer comes tomorrow. That's day two hundred forty-four.

sources.ref: Kena Upanishad 3.7–3.12 (Vayu; Indra; the being vanishes; Uma Haimavati)
